6fd74311.title: 1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond #Shorts
6fd74311.summary: The dolphin Short most likely broke out because YouTube's Shorts feed tested it with a wider French-speaking audience and people kept watching. The likely reason they kept watching is the opening line: it says a wild animal has a human trait, a first name, and answers to it, which raises a question viewers want answered. The crow tool-making Short broke out the next day with the same 'an animal does a human thing' idea, so this looks like a repeatable topic rather than luck. The octopus and tardigrade Shorts, which were about body facts rather than minds, stayed at the usual level.
6fd74311.report:
## The numbers

- **How far above usual:** 966 views against a usual 9, about 107 times the norm.
- **Not a one-off:** the next day, '1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie' reached 1,215 views. That makes 2 breakouts out of 6 Shorts in 48 hours.
- **The ones that stayed normal:** octopus (9 views), tardigrades (12), chimpanzee Ayumu (4) and elephant (0).
- **Likes per 100 views:** dolphin 5.2 and crow 4.1. The four normal Shorts together have 5 likes on 25 views, about 20 per 100. That high rate on a tiny base is what you see when only subscribers or friends watch. A stranger audience liking at 4-5 per 100 is a healthy rate.
- **Comments:** 0 on the dolphin and 1 on the crow, even though the script planned a pinned question. **Guess:** the pinned comment was never posted, or the question ('what would your whistle sound like?') was too abstract to answer.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics returned no retention, traffic sources or countries. So I can't confirm the share of Shorts-feed traffic, the swipe-away rate or which countries watched. The Ayumu and elephant Shorts may have been only hours old when the data was pulled, so their low counts don't prove anything yet. My web search hit its limit, so I could not check news or trends for 26 October. The timing points below are reasoning, not confirmed facts.

## Hook and first 2 seconds

The opening is 'Ce dauphin a un prénom. Et il répond quand on l'appelle.' It works for three reasons:
- It is short: two sentences of plain words.
- It says something surprising as plain fact, not as a question.
- It comes with a dolphin leaping from the water and the on-screen text « Ce dauphin a un PRÉNOM. »

The viewer knows the promise in under 2 seconds. Compare the hooks that stayed flat: 'three hearts' and 'tardigrades survived UV' are anatomy facts, interesting but with no 'that's like me' moment. The crow hook (an animal bends a wire into a tool) uses the same mechanism as the dolphin one.

## Psychology

- **Seeing ourselves in the animal (watch):** a first name is one of the most human things there is. Giving it to a wild animal creates instant surprise and doubt ('really?').
- **Curiosity gap (finish):** the 'how do they know?' question only pays off at about 0:24-0:34, when the synthetic copy without the dolphin's voice reveals that the name is in the melody. **Guess:** this halfway reveal kept people watching to the end.
- **Emotion near the end (like):** the 20-year memory of old companions adds warmth and a sense of loyalty, which is a typical reason people like a video.
- **Share:** **guess** — parents sending it to children, or friends sending a 'did you know' fact, helped by the family audience during the autumn school holidays.
- **Comment:** the closing question ('would you recognise a friend's voice after 20 years?') is personal but low-energy. Nobody answered it.

## Topic and timing

The topic is animal intelligence, and specifically animals that have names. The same idea already came back in widely covered studies: elephants (2024), marmosets (2024) and dolphins (2013). It is an evergreen hit, and the science is solid (King & Janik, PNAS 2013).

Timing: it went out on Monday 26 October at 13:29 Paris time (17:59 IST) and 08:29 in Quebec. **Guess:** French Toussaint holidays (about 17 Oct–2 Nov) and Belgian autumn holidays were probably on, meaning more family viewing in the daytime. But the octopus Short went out 1h45 earlier on the same day and stayed flat, so the time slot was not the cause. I can't tell when it took off or which countries watched without analytics. I found no news peak linked to dolphins (search unavailable).

## Title, description and thumbnail

- **Title:** '1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond' follows a clear equation format: a simple unit = a human trait, then the animal doing an action in the present tense. The crow title has the same structure ('1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie').
- **Failed titles also used numbers**, so numbers are not what made the difference. The difference: the breakout titles name a **human-like ability**, while '0,2 seconde, 5 chiffres' sounds like data, not an action.
- **Description:** dense, with sources and a clear note that the images illustrate rather than show the real experiment. That builds trust, but probably did not drive views.
- **Thumbnail:** barely matters in the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm

**Guess, based on how breakouts usually look on a channel with almost no subscribers:** nearly all views came from the Shorts feed. It probably went in waves: a small test group kept watching or looped, so YouTube widened the test, and growth then stopped near 1,000. Search and external links are unlikely at this volume. Check this in YouTube Studio (Reach > Traffic sources) as soon as the data is available.

## What did not matter

- Starting the title with a number: all six titles do it.
- The time of day (same day and same slot as a flop).
- The voice, the stock footage and the watermark, which are the same on every Short.
- The sources in the description.
- The comment question (0 replies).

## Repeat this

1. Topic: an animal shows a human ability (name, tool, memory, mourning, counting), backed by a well-known experiment.
2. Hook: one surprising statement in under 2 seconds, with the animal on screen and the key word in capitals.
3. A halfway reveal that explains how scientists proved it.
4. Title: '1 [thing] = 1 [human trait] : ce [animal] [verb]'.

## Test next

- Elephant names (already published): compare it with the dolphin at 48 hours to see whether the 'names' idea works again.
- Parrots naming their chicks, crows recognising faces, mourning in orcas.
- A comment question with two easy options ('yes / no', 'dolphin or crow?') against an open question.
- A 35-40 s version against the 55 s version, to measure completion rates.

changes.rule: Make at least half of all new Short topics animals showing one human-like mental ability (names, tool making, face recognition, long memory, mourning, counting), each based on one well-known peer-reviewed experiment you can name.
Make the first line a statement of 8 words or fewer that gives a specific animal a human trait, said as a fact ('Ce dauphin a un prénom.'), with no number, date or scientist's name before second 3.
Place the 'how did they prove it' twist between 40% and 60% of the script, and end with a yes/no or two-choice question the viewer can answer in one word.
Open on the animal in motion, framed close, from frame 1, with the hook word in capitals on screen; show the experiment's reveal (copy, tool, test) as a single clear visual at the halfway point.
Write titles in the form '1 [thing] = 1 [human trait] : ce/le [animal] [action verb] #Shorts', always naming the human trait in plain words, never two figures or a measurement.
Tag every Short as 'mind' (animal mental ability) or 'body' (anatomy/survival), and after 48 hours compare views and likes per 100 views for the two groups before choosing the next week's topic mix.

Also create a public playlist « Intelligence animale », add the dolphin, crow, Ayumu and elephant Shorts to it, and check Analytics > Traffic sources and Geography for the dolphin Short once they appear.

35417b59.title: 1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie #Shorts
35417b59.summary: The crow Short broke out because it promises one clear, visible transformation (a straight wire becomes a hook) and shows it in the first 4 seconds, about one of the internet's best-loved 'smart animal' species. Its sister breakout, the dolphin Short, used the same '1 X, 1 Y: this animal does a human thing' pattern. That suggests the Shorts feed is rewarding this format, not the topic area or the publish hour. Retention, traffic and country data are still empty, so how it was distributed is a well-supported guess.
35417b59.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 1,215 against a usual 9, about **135×**. Only one other Short got near it: the dolphin Short (966 views, published the day before). The other four got 0–12 views.
- **Likes:** 50, so **4.1 per 100 views**. The dolphin Short had 5.2. The four non-breakouts together had 5 likes on 25 views (20 per 100). That rate is inflated by tiny samples, probably the team and early followers, so it isn't a fair comparison. 4% is a healthy rate for Shorts-feed traffic.
- **Comments:** 1, so 0.08 per 100 views. The 'compréhension ou habitude ?' prompt barely worked.
- **A detail to watch:** both breakouts stopped at exactly 50 likes. That may be a coincidence. Check it isn't a display or caching artefact.
- **What we can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics totals, traffic and countries are empty. We don't know average view duration, % viewed, swipe-away rate, whether the views came from France or abroad, or how many came from the Shorts feed versus search. Everything below about distribution is inference.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is « Un seul fil de fer, bien droit. Ce corbeau le tord… et en fait un crochet. » It shows the whole story in one visual change: straight wire, then a hook. The on-screen text « 1 fil droit → 1 crochet » repeats the title word for word, so the promise in the feed matches the payoff on screen. It uses the present tense and the pointer word 'ce corbeau', which feels like watching it happen live, not hearing a lecture. The non-breakouts opened on abstract facts: three hearts, UV in orbit, 0.2 seconds. None of those can be seen in one image.

## Psychology
- **Watch:** surprise that an animal does something people thought only humans do (making a tool, not just using one). This is the same 'animal like us' pull that made the dolphin 'prénom' Short work.
- **Finish:** a curiosity gap opens at 0:36 (as smart as a 5–7-year-old?) and gets a twist at 0:44 (the results changed). That twist is a good reason to stay to the end. This is a guess until we have retention data.
- **Like:** quiet admiration plus 'learned something solid'.
- **Comment:** weak. A one-word answer to an academic question gives viewers no personal stake.
- **Share:** probably low. With no data, assume most reach came from the algorithm, not from sharing.

## Topic and timing
The crow that solves problems is a lasting viral genre. TikTok has whole discovery pages for 'smart crow videos', and clips such as a crow sledding on a roof lid (BoingBoing, June 2026) and a crow building a perch to drink (Upworthy) went viral this year. Futura-Sciences published a French piece on crow intelligence about two weeks before. A new German study saying crows make some visual decisions about twice as fast as humans was in the news around the same days. Whether that boosted us is a guess. Halloween week may also slightly favour crow imagery (guess).

Published 15:03 IST = **10:33 Paris** on a Tuesday. The script asked for 15 h or 21 h Paris. It looks like the time was entered as IST. When it took off and which countries watched are unknown until analytics fill in.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title « 1 fil de fer, 1 crochet : le corbeau qui plie » has the same shape as the dolphin winner « 1 sifflement = 1 prénom : ce dauphin répond »: two '1's, a concrete object, then the animal plus a present-tense action verb.

The losers break that shape:
- 'pourquoi' sounds like an explainer (octopus)
- a past-tense news report (tardigrades)
- a proper name nobody knows (Ayumu)

The description is careful and well sourced, but on the Shorts feed few viewers read it. It builds trust; it doesn't create reach. The planned thumbnail matters little on the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm
A guess: with 9 usual views and no outside push, 1,215 views almost certainly came from the **Shorts feed** testing it on new viewers and seeing enough watch time and likes to widen it. Search for 'corbeau' is possible but small. Suggested and external traffic are likely close to zero. Confirm in Analytics → Traffic source.

## What did not matter
- **Hashtags:** the same on every Short, losers included.
- **Sources and AI labels:** the same on every Short.
- **Narrator voice and music:** the same.
- **The subscribe call to action:** the same.
- **Publish hour:** the octopus Short at 11:46 Paris died, and the crow at 10:33 broke out. That weakly suggests the hour didn't matter.
- **The comment question:** 1 comment.
- **Two posts on one day:** the chimp Short, 4 hours after the crow, got 4 views. It probably didn't hurt the crow.

## Repeat this
- An animal doing one **human-like act you can see**, shown in full within 4 s.
- The title shape '1 X, 1 Y : ce/le [animal] qui [verbe au présent]'.
- On-screen text identical to the title's equation.
- Famous 'smart' species: corvids, dolphins, parrots, great apes, elephants.
- A twist near the end that makes viewers doubt what they just learned.

## Test next
- Does the elephant Short (same shape, ending in '?') perform like the dolphin? Its 0 views so far are too early to judge.
- Replace the academic one-word question with a personal one, e.g. 'Votre chien ferait-il ça ?'.
- End on the opening image (the hook) so the Short loops.
- Publish at real 15 h Paris to compare with the 10:33 slot.

changes.rule: Pick topics where a well-known 'smart' animal (crow, raven, parrot, dolphin, great ape, elephant) does one human-like act that can be shown in a single before/after image, such as making a tool, answering to a name or counting. Skip topics that are only a body fact or a lab statistic.

Make the first sentence deliver the whole act in under 4 seconds: one object, one action, one result, in the present tense with 'ce [animal]'. Example: 'Un seul fil droit. Ce corbeau le tord… et en fait un crochet.'

Replace the abstract closing question with a personal, easy one that refers to the viewer's own life or pet (e.g. 'Votre chien ferait-il ça ? Oui ou non'). Make the very last line point back to the opening image so the Short loops.

Open the first 2 seconds on the before→after change itself (e.g. straight wire, then hook), with on-screen text '1 X → 1 Y' matching the title word for word. Never open on a title card, a map or a scientist.
Write titles in the form '1 [objet], 1 [résultat] : ce/le [animal] qui [verbe au présent] #Shorts'. Never use 'pourquoi', the past tense or an unknown proper name (like Ayumu) in the title.

Tag every Short as 'equation format' or 'other'. Each day, compare views and likes per 100 views for the two groups, and the elephant Short against the dolphin and crow winners, once YouTube Analytics retention and traffic data arrive.
Keep it narrator-only for animal-intelligence Shorts. Give the animal its real name (like Betty) only in the second sentence, after the hook has shown what it did.

e7a70ed3.title: 3 करोड़ वोटर कटे? याचिकाकर्ता का दावा, SC का नोटिस #Shorts
e7a70ed3.summary: This Short got about 10 times the channel's usual views (78 against 8) because it was posted the same night the Supreme Court issued notice on Maharashtra's voter-list revision (SIR). It was also the only recent Short where the viewer had something personal at stake: the question of whether their own name had been cut from the voter list. The English version of the same story beat the channel's other English Short too (20 views against 0), so the topic drove the breakout, not the language or the presentation. These counts are very small, though, and there is no analytics data yet, so treat this as an early signal rather than proof.
e7a70ed3.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 78 against a usual 8, about 9.8 times normal. The English twin of the same story, posted at the same minute, got 20. The other English Short (electoral bonds) got 0, so the English version also did far better than its comparison. The Hindi Shorts that did not break out got 7 (BRICS) and 9 (electoral bonds).
- **Comments:** 2 comments, about 2.6 per 100 views. Every other Short on the channel has 0 comments. This is the only Short so far that got people to reply.
- **Likes:** 0 per 100 views. The electoral-bonds Short got 1 like on 9 views. At these sample sizes, likes tell us nothing.
- **Retention, traffic sources, countries:** all empty in the data. We cannot yet say whether people watched to the end, whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, or whether viewers were in Maharashtra. A spike to 78 is the size of one small test batch that YouTube sends to the Shorts feed (a guess). It could also be a few search clicks on 'SIR'. What we can't know yet: average % viewed, swipe-away rate, how many views came from search, and whether the 2 comments came from real viewers or from the team.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script in the data, so this section is a guess based on the title. The opening most likely showed the number '3 करोड़' together with the question 'वोटर कटे?'. A big round number plus a question makes the viewer ask 'is that me?' in under a second. The BRICS and electoral-bonds Shorts open on events that don't touch the viewer's life today. Next time we need the script and the retention curve to confirm the hook did the work.

## Psychology
- **Personal stake and fear of loss:** the description says about one in three Maharashtra voters were cut. People respond more strongly to losing something they already have (their vote) than to news about spending or about past verdicts.
- **An open question that makes people keep watching:** the claim, the court notice, the Election Commission not yet answering, and a next hearing on 5 November. The story is unfinished, which is a reason to watch to the end and to comment.
- **Reassurance worth sharing:** the Chief Justice said no one would be prosecuted for filling Form 6, the form deleted voters are being asked to use. That is useful to forward to family (a guess on sharing; we have no share data).
- **Comment prompt:** the closing question ('क्या कोर्ट के फ़ैसले तक नाम कटना रुकना चाहिए?' – should the deletions stop until the court decides?) is a yes/no question anyone can answer. That probably explains the 2 comments.

## Topic and timing
The Supreme Court issued notice to the Election Commission, the Centre and Maharashtra on Monday 26 October without granting interim relief (LiveLaw, The Wire, Deccan Herald). The Short went up at 22:38 IST the same day, while people were still searching for the news. SIR deletions had been a national story for weeks: Rahul Gandhi's plea, the Delhi Form-6 matter and the Uttar Pradesh deletions. So the subject already had an audience, and the court notice was a fresh trigger.

**Accuracy flag:** Deccan Herald and The Federal report about **2.07 crore (21.14%)** names dropped from the draft rolls. '3 crore / one in three' is the petitioner's figure, close to The Wire's one-third estimate against 2024 electors. The description correctly says the figures are the petitioner's. The title, however, leads with the larger, contested number. To stay neutral, the official figure has to appear alongside the claim. We have no country data, but a mostly Indian audience, concentrated in Maharashtra, is a likely guess.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title has a number, a question mark, who is claiming it, and what the institution did. The question mark plus 'याचिकाकर्ता का दावा' (the petitioner's claim) keeps it neutral. It leaves out 'महाराष्ट्र' (Maharashtra) and 'SIR', the words people actually search for, although the hashtags cover SIR. The description is strong: it names its sources, gives the next date and ends on a question. The thumbnail is irrelevant on the Shorts feed.

## Audience and algorithm
There is no traffic data. My best guess: the Shorts feed tested the video on Hindi news viewers, and comments that came in early helped it get a second batch. Search for 'SIR', 'voter list' and 'Supreme Court' on the night of the hearing may have added views. There is no sign of external sharing.

## What did not matter
- **Language alone:** both language versions did better than their comparison Shorts.
- **Publish hour:** 22:38 is late, and the BRICS Short at 01:19 still failed. Being on the same day as the news mattered, not the clock time.
- **Likes:** zero, yet the video still spread.
- **Accountability framing by itself:** the BRICS Short ('क्या ख़र्च जनता को बताया जाएगा?' – will the spending be disclosed to the public?) asked an accountability question but had no personal stake for the viewer.
- **Old verdicts:** electoral bonds is a settled story, and it did not spread.

## Repeat this
- Post the same day as a court or Election Commission action.
- Pick topics where the viewer can ask 'does this affect me?'.
- Lead with one big number, labelled as a claim.
- End on the next date and a yes/no question.
- Name every source.

## Test next
- Put 'महाराष्ट्र SIR' in the title, against the current style.
- Open with 'क्या आपका नाम कटा?' (has your name been cut?) and how to check (electoralsearch.eci.gov.in), against opening on the number.
- Post a follow-up Short on the 5 November hearing and on the final roll, to see whether a running story keeps its viewers.
- Get the retention and traffic data exported for this video and the next ones.

changes.rule: Each day, choose at least one topic that is a court, Election Commission or government action from the last 24 hours that directly affects an ordinary voter's own rights, documents or deadlines (voter list, Aadhaar, Form 6, a scheme cut-off). Rank these above summits, spending stories and past verdicts.

Open the script with one big number framed as a question the viewer can relate to (for example, 'क्या आपका नाम भी कटा?'). If that number comes from a party or petitioner, give the officially reported figure in the very next sentence, with both sources named (for example: 3 crore per the petitioner, about 2.07 crore per the draft-roll reports).

End every Short on the next official date (hearing, deadline, final list) and one neutral yes/no question viewers can answer in the comments. Where viewers have something to do, say how they can check or act (for example, 'नाम जाँचें: electoralsearch.eci.gov.in').

In the first second, put the key number and a question mark on screen in large Hindi text over a real Wikimedia photo of the institution (Supreme Court, Election Commission). Show a full-screen date card for the next hearing or deadline in the last 2 seconds.

Write titles in this pattern: '[number] [what happened]? [who claims it], [institution action]'. Include the state name and the term people search for (for example, 'महाराष्ट्र SIR') within the first 40 characters.

Have one anchor ask the viewer's personal question ('मेरा नाम कटा तो क्या करूँ?' – what do I do if my name was cut?) and the other answer only with sourced facts and the official step to take, never with an opinion.

Whenever a Short gets more than 3 times the usual views, schedule a follow-up Short on the same story's next official date (here: the 5 November SIR hearing and the final roll publication) and compare its views with the original.

650a68f1.title: चुनाव आयोग का सुप्रीम कोर्ट में जवाब: 3 SIR आदेश और Form 6 #Shorts
650a68f1.summary: The Short got 196 views against a usual 7 (28x). It came out about a day after a real news event: on Monday, 26 October, the Election Commission filed a reply in the Supreme Court defending CEC Gyanesh Kumar and its SIR decisions. The title used the same words people were already searching for (चुनाव आयोग, सुप्रीम कोर्ट, SIR, Form 6), stated the news plainly instead of asking a question, and was posted in Hindi in the early evening. Likes and comments were weak (1 like, 0 comments), so my best guess is that YouTube tested it with more viewers or it was found through search, not that viewers shared it widely.
650a68f1.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 196 against a usual 7, about 28x. The next best Short got 78 views (the Hindi '3 करोड़ वोटर कटे?' Short, 26 Oct), so this one did about 2.5x the channel's previous best.
- **Likes per 100 views:** 0.51 (1 like). The other Shorts together got 1 like on 114 views (0.88 per 100).
- **Comments per 100 views:** 0 here, against 1.75 for the rest of the channel (2 comments, both on the 78-view Short). The comment prompt in the description ('कमेंट में नंबर लिखें') got no replies.
- **Retention, traffic sources, countries:** all empty in this export.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** whether the views came in one burst (a single Shorts-feed test) or slowly from search, how many viewers swiped away before the 0:33–0:40 sponsor segment, and whether viewers were in India. Low likes and comments with high views usually mean the views came from people seeing it in the feed or search, not from people sharing it. **This is a guess until Studio shows the traffic sources.**

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script, so I can't check the opening line. The title already works as a hook: it names two big institutions (चुनाव आयोग, सुप्रीम कोर्ट), says something just happened ('जवाब'), and names two concrete things (3 SIR orders, Form 6). Most of the channel's other titles open with a question ('क्या…?', 'फ़ैसला किसका?'). **Guess:** if the first spoken line repeated the title's plain news ('चुनाव आयोग ने सुप्रीम कोर्ट से कहा…'), viewers had a reason to keep watching in the first 2 seconds.

## Psychology
The draw was a news gap: the Election Commission, the body under question, has now answered in court, and the court hasn't decided yet. People who have followed the SIR voter-list story since 2025 want to know what the Commission actually said. The description raised a second question (a news report counted about 14 objections by the commissioners vs. 'all three orders were unanimous'), but the comment prompt asked viewers to pick between two procedural points. That doesn't make anyone feel strongly, which fits the zero comments. Viewers watched for information, not to argue or to share.

## Topic and timing
The Statesman reported that on Monday, 26 Oct, the ECI filed a counter affidavit in the Supreme Court. It said all SIR decisions were unanimous, Form 6 was not modified, and the petition against CEC Gyanesh Kumar rests on a single news report. The Short went up at 18:18 IST on Tuesday, about a day later, while people were still searching the story. SIR is one of the few election-process topics with lasting Hindi search interest, because voters worry about their own names being cut from the rolls.

Timing alone doesn't explain the result. The electoral bonds Short went up 54 minutes earlier the same day and got 9 views. That topic is old: the verdict came in 2024. The BRICS Short (7 views, 01:19) and the English versions (20 and 0 views) also did poorly. The two Shorts posted at 02:30 and 03:06 on 28 Oct show 0 views, but they may simply be too new at the time of this export. There is no country data. **Guess:** almost all views came from India.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** a plain news headline that starts with the names people search for. It matches how Hindi news headlines covered the story, so it can show up in search and in suggestions next to those news videos.
- **Description:** the first line after 'Brands: DM us…' repeats the keywords (ECI, SIR, Form 6, फ़ाइल नोट), lists two sources and clearly says the court hasn't ruled. That helps search and keeps the channel neutral.
- **Brand line:** 'Brands: DM us' as the opening line uses up the preview text. It didn't stop this breakout, but it is the weakest part of the description.
- **Thumbnail:** not meaningful for Shorts in the feed.
- **Sources:** LiveLaw plus Organiser is a lopsided source pair for a neutral channel. Pairing LiveLaw with a wire service or a mainstream paper is safer.

## Audience and algorithm
**Guess, in order of likelihood:**
1. The Shorts feed showed it to a test batch of Hindi viewers who watch politics and court news. Because the topic was fresh, enough of them watched to earn a second batch, and then it stopped because nobody liked, commented or shared.
2. Some views came from YouTube search for 'चुनाव आयोग सुप्रीम कोर्ट' or 'SIR Form 6'.

There is no sign of external traffic. The Hindi version of the voter-cut story beat its English twin 78 to 20, which supports keeping Shorts in Hindi only, as the channel says it does.

## What did not matter
- The comment prompt (0 replies).
- Hashtags: the electoral bonds Short used the same style and got 9.
- The Wikimedia photo of the Supreme Court.
- The sample sponsor segment and the AI disclosure: neither stopped the breakout.
- Posting time on its own: a Short 54 minutes earlier the same day got 9 views.
- English versions: weaker every time.

## Repeat this
- Choose a court filing, hearing or official reply from the last 24–36 hours that names a known institution.
- Write the title as a plain statement: 'संस्था का मंच पर जवाब: संख्या + दस्तावेज़' (institution's reply at a forum: number + document).
- Use the exact Hindi words people search for.
- Say clearly in the Short that the court hasn't ruled yet.
- Post in Hindi, early evening IST.
- Follow the same story when the next step happens.

## Test next
- **Statement vs. question:** compare '3 चुनाव आयुक्त, फ़ैसला किसका?' (question, 03:06) with this Short. Then publish the next SIR follow-up with a statement-style title between 17:00 and 20:00 IST and compare.
- **Sponsor placement:** run one Short with the sponsor segment after the main point and the open question, at the very end, and see whether retention improves.
- **Comment prompt:** replace the A/B choice with a question about the viewer's own experience, e.g. 'क्या आपका नाम वोटर लिस्ट में जाँचा गया?' (Has your name been checked on the voter list?), and see whether comments rise.
- **Studio check:** after 48 hours, read the traffic sources to confirm or reject the feed-vs-search guess.
